title: The Sundanese script
goal: Read street, office and station signs in West Java written in Sundanese script, and write your own name in it.
bekal: the seven aksara swara (vowels) and twenty-three aksara ngalagena (consonants)

notes: **Aksara Sunda Baku** (standard Sundanese script) was set in 1997 and made official by a West Java regional regulation in 2003. Since then, street signs, government offices and stations across West Java must show it beneath the Latin writing.
**Teu pati** = not too, not very. It pairs with *pati*, "too": *teu pati hésé* = not too hard. It's a very common, handy way to soften a judgment.

**Sadulur** = related, like siblings. Sundanese script really is a relative of Javanese script (Hanacaraka) and Balinese script: all three descend from Kawi script, which comes from the Pallava script of southern India.
**Nambahan** comes from *tambah* + *N-* + *-an* = to add to. Compare *nambahkeun* (to add something): the endings *-an* and *-keun* change the direction of the action, as you learned in Unit 10.
**Panghulu** is the name of one of the marks in Sundanese script: the one that changes the *a* sound to *i*. You'll meet the names of all these marks in the next table.
⚠️ Don't be discouraged if you feel slow: most Sundanese people read this script slowly too. The goal of this unit isn't fluency. It's making signs stop being just pictures.

grammars.title: How Sundanese script works
body: Sundanese script is an **abugida**, not an alphabet. The difference matters: every consonant letter already carries the vowel *a*. The letter ᮊ isn't read "k" but **ka**. To change the vowel, you add a small mark called a **rarangkén**.
after: Thirteen marks sounds like a lot, but the first six cover almost every sign you'll read: *panghulu*, *panyuku*, *panéléng*, *panolong*, *pamepet* and *pamaéh*.
⚠️ **Pamaéh** (᮪) is the most important one for reading signs, because it kills the built-in vowel. Without it, you'd read *Bandung* as *Bandunga*.

If the script on this page shows up as empty boxes on your device, the Sundanese font isn't installed. Recent Android phones and iPhones have it; on older devices, install *Noto Sans Sundanese* from Google Fonts.

blocks.text: **Aksara swara** are the seven stand-alone vowel letters, used when a word begins with a vowel:
**Aksara ngalagena** are the consonant letters, each already carrying the sound *a*. The first eighteen are native Sundanese letters; the last five were added for loanwords.

⚠️ The order isn't a-b-c; it follows sound groups, and schoolchildren in West Java learn it as a chant: *ka-ga-nga, ca-ja-nya, ta-da-na, pa-ba-ma, ya-ra-la, wa-sa-ha*. Six groups of three, eighteen native letters. Once you know those six lines, you've mastered the hardest part.
Now the useful part. Here are names that really appear on signs in and around Bandung, broken down syllable by syllable:

blocks.text: Notice the recurring pattern: many Sundanese place names start with **Ci-** (from *cai*, water) and **Pa-**. Once you can spot those two opening syllables in the script (ᮎᮤ and ᮕ), half the signs in West Java become readable.

blocks.title: The most useful five-minute practice
items: Learn the six ngalagena lines as a chant: *ka-ga-nga · ca-ja-nya · ta-da-na · pa-ba-ma · ya-ra-la · wa-sa-ha*.
Learn just three marks first: **panghulu** (i), **panyuku** (u), **pamaéh** (kills the vowel).
Every time you pass a street sign, read the bottom line before looking at the top line. Check your answer.
Write your own name. That's the first word that will stick.
Don't chase speed. The goal isn't fluent reading; it's no longer seeing the script as decoration.
